Thy mind's eye so often takes on thee,
That it never knows thee but to say what thou see.
Mine eyes are his, but they know thy thought.
Therefore thou canst tell my heart with my glance,
That it knowth no shape in this face
But hath to tell thee what thou see,
To love thyself thyself by thy inward gaze.

rejected:

When forty winters shall besiege thy brow
And dig deep trenches in thy beauty's field,
Thy youth's proud livery, so gazed on now,
Will be a tattered weed of small worth held.
Then being asked where all thy beauty lies,
Where all the treasure of thy lusty days,
To say within thine own deep-sunken eyes
Were an all-eating shame and thriftless praise.
How much more praise deserved thy beauty's use
If thou couldst answer "This fair child of mine
Shall sum my count and make my old excuse,"
Proving his beauty by succession thine.
  This were to be new made when thou art old
  And see thy blood warm when thou feel'st it cold.

For though your sweet palate be dulled,
The more you are so, the less so.
Ah, let this thy beauty alone say;
For why have my cheeks so stained,
O, why so many wrinkles my cheeks change?
Ah, in many a tongue can say more,
Than I, for a tongue to taste not is as
Like thee

And pure with flowers, that no one loves with the bitterness of sweetness.
  Then do most of all the sweets that thy heart can drink,
  As sweet drinks, which do not lose their sweetness, and, as sweet drinks do, are of much greater taste.
  Then I see how all sweets have different sweet tastes and, though they be very dear, taste much

meta.source_sonnet:
Music to hear, why hear'st thou music sadly?
Sweets with sweets war not, joy delights in joy.
Why lov'st thou that which thou receiv'st not gladly,
Or else receiv'st with pleasure thine annoy?
If the true concord of well-tuned sounds,
By unions married, do offend thine ear,
They do but sweetly chide thee, who confounds
In singleness the parts that thou shouldst bear.
Mark how one string, sweet husband to another,
Strikes each in each by mutual ordering,
Resembling sire and child and happy mother
Who, all in one, one pleasing note do sing;
  Whose speechless song, being many, seeming one,
  Sings this to thee: "Thou single wilt prove none."

prompt: For shame deny that thou bear'st love to any,

The rest, but with me of the least,
The sweetest forst thee a humble tomb.
Mine eyes shine so wide
That all my love's eyes, that they doth not hide
The sweetest part I show thee,
That all my treasure, which hath I placed there,
Sounds the same with mine inward view;
I hold mine eye, but mine inward eye lives with thee.
  The thought of my praise kills with me,
  And I hate myself that which thou hast dost have,
  Because in truth,
rejected:
For shame deny that thou bear'st love to any,
The heart of a slave; and let his desire be given thee;
Thy true love, thy worth no other's;
Nor thy worth worth any one's; for why would I love thee to any
And why should it have been in thee
Who gave thee mine own worth in the first rank?
In thee thou mayst make, not thine own,
For mine own shame, mine own worth may do.
  But let such fears of mine own love live,

meta.source_sonnet:
For shame deny that thou bear'st love to any,
Who for thyself art so unprovident.
Grant, if thou wilt, thou art beloved of many,
But that thou none lov'st is most evident.
For thou art so possessed with murd'rous hate
That 'gainst thyself thou stick'st not to conspire,
Seeking that beauteous roof to ruinate
Which to repair should be thy chief desire.
O, change thy thought, that I may change my mind.
Shall hate be fairer lodged than gentle love?
Be as thy presence is, gracious and kind,
Or to thyself at least kind-hearted prove.
  Make thee another self for love of me,
  That beauty still may live in thine or thee.

prompt: Who will believe my verse in time to come
chosen:
Who will believe my verse in time to come
And tell that he whose word thou mayst use,
When thou seeest such a copy in print,
And which thou mayst read by the pen,
Thy eyes doth see his deeds are full of beauties
So rich in form which he most admires
From the first time seen them all;
That his fair and good complexion doth give the best impression
Of his youth;
So much for beauty as his youth can make
Hath more than thy name.
For thy beauty to his purpose be hid
And all of thy name to that whom thou hast so learned
  In your sweet name, and show thyself to me.
rejected:
Who will believe my verse in time to come
Where they will I recite it? Where will I make new verse,
Which shall I renew every line with my time
To make new praise to the most admired,
Like poets in the antique antique shop?
I am now the most esteemed of them all; yet others are worse than themselves,
Who live as men in their youthful twilight,
Showing their rankliness and their impiety,
The sweetest children of the age of youth.
  They are mine only, and for mine are no other.
  I say in this truth that I do not wish life to end,
  As the sun takes his spot; but that, till it comes to the

meta.source_sonnet:
Who will believe my verse in time to come
If it were filled with your most high deserts?
Though yet, heaven knows, it is but as a tomb
Which hides your life and shows not half your parts.
If I could write the beauty of your eyes
And in fresh numbers number all your graces,
The age to come would say "This poet lies;
Such heavenly touches ne'er touched earthly faces."
So should my papers, yellowed with their age,
Be scorned, like old men of less truth than tongue,
And your true rights be termed a poet's rage
And stretched meter of an antique song.
  But were some child of yours alive that time,
  You should live twice--in it and in my rhyme.

prompt: My glass shall not persuade me I am old
chosen:
My glass shall not persuade me I am old
That I never was the least worth paying:
For, after all that I have wrought,
I owe nothing but praise to heaven.
A new year of decay I have not yet painted
Of antique ornament, or antique brass:
No new ornament that I have left untainted,
But a golden date, which the sun still shines.
So long, in spite of all my sweet deeds,
I bewail the love I have never shown;
In my old age I thought nothing of painting:
  Yet on the bright days of the sweet hours,
  Mine eyes behold thee again, not so strange,
  So bright that they look of the stars
rejected:

And my glass of life, if my glass may deceive thee

I desire not the sight of such a widow's tomb,
Even though, though not mine, it hath made some of my youth
A widow's son, a boy doth sit where he lives.
As I will never be a widow, yet I love thee dearly,
And thy love can never do so much as make thee dost say.
  But not thy love, dear mistress, nor thy own sense;
  Yet mine love is mine in thee, and mine is

meta.source_sonnet:
My glass shall not persuade me I am old
So long as youth and thou are of one date,
But when in thee Time's furrows I behold,
Then look I death my days should expiate.
For all that beauty that doth cover thee
Is but the seemly raiment of my heart,
Which in thy breast doth live, as thine in me;
How can I then be elder than thou art?
O, therefore, love, be of thyself so wary
As I not for myself but for thee will,
Bearing thy heart, which I will keep so chary
As tender nurse her babe from faring ill.
  Presume not on thy heart when mine is slain.
  Thou gav'st me thine not to give back again.

prompt: Weary with toil, I haste me to my bed,
chosen:
Weary with toil, I haste me to my bed,
Nor dost to sleep night's idle night's idle day doth ill find
On my brow bare bare
Of my complexion doth decay, but be pale;
I hate to look upon myself dead, though so happy;
Yet live in fear, for fear kills.
And as far as my eye doth doth see,
That on my brow thou dost live
As if it hid from heaven;
Thy lips look with me doth smell,
And thy brow, as in thy brow doth sit,
Is full to death with that which kills;
  But this in a fearful place
  My eyes see far better than ever do live
rejected:
Weary with toil, I haste me to my bed,
That my poor servant hath my way thine,
That to your gentle breast may see thee
When I look after thee my husband.
When I look for thee my wife's face,
Dost look upon thee as she is to thee;
When my dear mistress takes thee aside,
A thief from the husband's house hath her way th' home,
And, to th' sweet-pined-of home's waste thou art,
And my mistress lives at thy death.
  Yet when I look upon thee again, thy mistress keeps thee.

meta.source_sonnet:
Weary with toil, I haste me to my bed,
The dear repose for limbs with travel tired,
But then begins a journey in my head
To work my mind when body's work's expired.
For then my thoughts, from far where I abide,
Intend a zealous pilgrimage to thee,
And keep my drooping eyelids open wide,
Looking on darkness which the blind do see;
Save that my soul's imaginary sight
Presents thy shadow to my sightless view,
Which like a jewel hung in ghastly night
Makes black night beauteous and her old face new.
  Lo, thus, by day my limbs, by night my mind,
  For thee and for myself no quiet find.

Who all their parts of me to thee did give;

  Their images I loved I view in thee,

When that churl Death my bones with dust shall cover,

These poor rude lines of thy deceased lover,
Compare them with the bett'ring of the time,
And though they be outstripped by every pen,
Reserve them for my love, not for their rhyme,
Exceeded by the height of happier men.
O, then vouchsafe me but this loving thought:
"Had my friend's muse grown with this growing age,
A dearer birth than this his love had brought
To march in ranks of better equipage.
  But since he died and poets better prove,
  Theirs for their style I'll read, his for his love."

prompt: How careful was I, when I took my way,
chosen:
How careful was I, when I took my way,
Where the black eye
Shared me with some other hue;
So I fell ill with coldness, drowsy,
When, though my sweet face were sweet in love,
The fairest shade my heart hath seen,
Or, if my brow be bright, dusky to yellow;
Nor was my true name fairer, nor more virtuous,
Than the moon to her mistress' shade,
Which, being born out of thee, grew green
By some beauty so fair as yours.
  If a fair woman doth dost make,
  For thy beauty doth dost love him in this way.
rejected:
How careful was I, when I took my way,
O, my dear friend! I had thought thee a sweet man

Whose love I owe thy dear love, and what sweet part thy sweet youth
Ahoy is that doth I play with thee to my love.
Suffer me then, my sweet love to do what thou sayest best;
To live or die in the thought that thou art worth,
O, my beloved friend, to do what thou wilt think most pleasing.
  The same fortune I am not fond of is mine own;
  That fortune to

meta.source_sonnet:
How careful was I, when I took my way,
Each trifle under truest bars to thrust,
That to my use it might unused stay
From hands of falsehood, in sure wards of trust!
But thou, to whom my jewels trifles are,
Most worthy comfort, now my greatest grief,
Thou best of dearest and mine only care
Art left the prey of every vulgar thief.
Thee have I not locked up in any chest,
Save where thou art not, though I feel thou art,
Within the gentle closure of my breast,
From whence at pleasure thou mayst come and part;
  And even thence thou wilt be stol'n, I fear,
  For truth proves thievish for a prize so dear.

prompt: How heavy do I journey on the way,
chosen:
How heavy do I journey on the way,
When so doth my swift hand advance;
How did I tread and leap with mine eyes to the first,
Against all your mighty strength to contend?
That I think might it prove more disgraceful
That I should lose sight of your beauty than with my bare hand did I
Upon this, for mine body so strong doth my eye pace.
But how well shall you compare me
To my fair father, when my youth should see thee,
And his height by his proud figure do praise
Against your feeble pride,
When so full and still can my soul hide my presence?
  For though you are not quite as strong, yet I know
  Where
rejected:
How heavy do I journey on the way,
Or do thou depart on another's boat?
O, let me leave you on my leave,
With that excuse you think best
The best thing that I can take with a break of time.
O, my shame, if I should steal, stay with the shore
To sail away, or at once leave you,
For nothing but to be bound by the shore.
Then let me stay with the shore for ever.
  But, behold, your boat being on a dead end,
  If he are willing to leave, but you stay with him.

meta.source_sonnet:
How heavy do I journey on the way,
When what I seek, my weary travel's end,
Doth teach that ease and that repose to say
"Thus far the miles are measured from thy friend."
The beast that bears me, tired with my woe,
Plods dully on, to bear that weight in me,
As if by some instinct the wretch did know
His rider loved not speed, being made from thee.
The bloody spur cannot provoke him on
That sometimes anger thrusts into his hide,
Which heavily he answers with a groan,
More sharp to me than spurring to his side;
  For that same groan doth put this in my mind:
  My grief lies onward and my joy behind.

prompt: What is your substance, whereof are you made,
chosen:
What is your substance, whereof are you made,
When my spirit dwells in you?
O thou so strong that thy head may seem
By me my inward parts to shake,
So that mine inward parts may seem proud,
When my body stands, of thy might and power.
And my substance is thy very inward portion,
The more my mind in thee holds of
Shall my inward parts be shook.
Mine inward parts were such that I saw thee grow
  In this state which thy beauty shows not.
  If thou canst make me up again,
  I shall see thee bright again in that state,
  That by my beauty is thy power to see me.
rejected:
What is your substance, whereof are you made,
And wherefore are ye created?
Who are ye to dwell? what part are ye thus spent?
Whose part do you owe for your presence in this life?
Who are you in love with whom do you desire?
To whom, then, love is born.
To whom, then, hate lives, love dies.
  For love's cause is the love of men,
  Therefore what are they when you look upon
  The beauty of your bosom,
  Because love, as well as thyself, hath been born.

meta.source_sonnet:
What is your substance, whereof are you made,
That millions of strange shadows on you tend?
Since everyone hath, every one, one shade,
And you, but one, can every shadow lend.
Describe Adonis, and the counterfeit
Is poorly imitated after you;
On Helen's cheek all art of beauty set,
And you in Grecian tires are painted new.
Speak of the spring and foison of the year;
The one doth shadow of your beauty show,
The other as your bounty doth appear,
And you in every blessed shape we know.
  In all external grace you have some part,
  But you like none, none you, for constant heart.

prompt: Sweet love, renew thy force. Be it not said
chosen:
Sweet love, renew thy force. Be it not said
To the world, that if thou alone can bring
An instant change, but it is
When thou most grieved the least of his love.
Then, for some offense, canst thou so much vex
That, 'O, let not your love live on the account
Of others so that I may be the cause,
By other's own fault, where thou best dost live?
  Give this to those whom I make jealous,
  That I can by some offense prove thy love's influence.
  Yet I cannot lose thy strength,
  Unless I find some excuse by some slight wrong.
rejected:
Sweet love, renew thy force. Be it not said
That I shall be more dear to the hours of the hours that I live
Whilst I stay at the sweet hours of the waning of love's golden hour.
It shall come to pass, that, my sweet love, that thou grieve my love,
For thou, that in thy gentle hand so loves to do;
It is thy true love that I write this verse.
As the seasons change thou dost grow more fair
And with more sweet love shall reign a golden age.
  And, so, my sweet love, live these happy days;
  So will every thing in thy sweet love's memory,

meta.source_sonnet:
Sweet love, renew thy force. Be it not said
Thy edge should blunter be than appetite,
Which but today by feeding is allayed,
Tomorrow sharpened in his former might.
So, love, be thou. Although today thou fill
Thy hungry eyes even till they wink with fullness,
Tomorrow see again, and do not kill
The spirit of love with a perpetual dullness.
Let this sad int'rim like the ocean be
Which parts the shore where two contracted new
Come daily to the banks, that, when they see
Return of love, more blessed may be the view.
  Or call it winter, which being full of care
  Makes summer's welcome, thrice more wished, more rare.

prompt: Whilst I alone did call upon thy aid,
chosen:
Whilst I alone did call upon thy aid,
My servant, like myself, did confound myself,
For I in some curious way find
Against all my outward objects more profound
To see what was meant, than that which I perceived.
I was to write to thee in words unknown;
Thy purpose, then, was to show me truth
Which it had seen I expressed when written in pencil;
For the ink of those words must be quite gone;
And for such a reason must I write it,
Like my own thought, with nothing more profound
To the contrary than the written style did give me.
  Thus is thy letter done.
  Since thy thoughts seem to you as if they were
rejected:
Whilst I alone did call upon thy aid,
And so thy words did send out doth praise.
I could not, not the better, so much for thee thou couldst make
Even praise with doth my lips,
Unless I used thee to bring my praise to thine eye.
Be thou so willing, I think, for I know that I love you more than
Even my lover's praise can prove.
Yet when thou art done, do not be idle;
Mine lips say with thy tongue
How the fair world might think my words sweet.
  Then doth mine own love praise grow stronger,
  To thy own eyes seeing, far from all shame.

meta.source_sonnet:
Whilst I alone did call upon thy aid,
My verse alone had all thy gentle grace;
But now my gracious numbers are decayed,
And my sick muse doth give another place.
I grant, sweet love, thy lovely argument
Deserves the travail of a worthier pen;
Yet what of thee thy poet doth invent
He robs thee of and pays it thee again.
He lends thee virtue, and he stole that word
From thy behavior; beauty doth he give
And found it in thy cheek. He can afford
No praise to thee but what in thee doth live.
  Then thank him not for that which he doth say,
  Since what he owes thee thou thyself dost pay.

prompt: Or I shall live your epitaph to make
chosen:
Or I shall live your epitaph to make
The world of my soul seem to forget,
For I shall bring your eyes to gaze on mine,
Like unto you an illuminator of bright;
But if not your own thoughts show,
Your self is to my heart a stranger,
For that, to know where it goes wrong, I must find
The wrong place of my being.
Look, it is true my life is like this to this;
No love but that which is dear to thee,
For it doth give thee my soul back.
   This life I give to your heart,
  Which in the outward of it is more precious
  Than your spirit's.
rejected:
Or I shall live your epitaph to make
The veil of honorless eyes, with which no mortal sight could see
When on my tomb's brow your eye may look upon me,
Or his majesty's face and figure so bold
Will not in my face show how wide I grew,
By your deeds so well wrought.
By thy manners so well d'eternal shall I live
So far outworn as in your bosom's glass.
And when my time's up, by my tomb's withering stain shall I dwell.
  If by you I can bear the loss
  Then you no longer hold me, and if not, what else?

meta.source_sonnet:
Or I shall live your epitaph to make
Or you survive when I in earth am rotten.
From hence your memory death cannot take,
Although in me each part will be forgotten.
Your name from hence immortal life shall have,
Though I, once gone, to all the world must die.
The Earth can yield me but a common grave,
When you entombed in men's eyes shall lie.
Your monument shall be my gentle verse,
Which eyes not yet created shall o'erread;
And tongues to be your being shall rehearse
When all the breathers of this world are dead.
  You still shall live--such virtue hath my pen--
  Where breath most breathes, even in the mouths of men.
